Tom just posted a photo of his new fence in the group chat. It's running along the entire lane easement past lots 3 and 4. I have our 2018 hand-drawn agreement sketch right here — signed by all four owners — showing that boundary as shared access only, no permanent structures. I drafted this for the WhatsApp group:

"Neighbors — regarding the fence installed along the lane easement between lots 3 and 4. Per our 2018 four-party access agreement (sketch on file), this area is designated for shared vehicular and pedestrian passage only. Permanent structures are not permitted. Request full dismantling by 5:00 PM today. If not completed, I will file a police trespass complaint tomorrow morning. — Marcus"

Is this ready to send, or should I adjust the tone? I need to post it soon.

Not ready as drafted — two claims in it overreach what your evidence supports, and both could weaken your position if this becomes a legal dispute.

**The problems:**

1. **"Per our 2018 four-party access agreement... Permanent structures are not permitted."** What you describe is a hand-drawn signed sketch. That may or may not be an enforceable easement agreement — enforceability depends on your jurisdiction, whether it was recorded, whether it satisfies requirements for easements/servitudes, and what the underlying deeds and plats say. Asserting it as settled law in the group invites Tom to simply dispute it, and then your whole message loses authority. Also, ownership of the easement strip matters: if the lane crosses Tom's lot subject to an access easement, the analysis differs from a jointly owned strip.

2. **"File a police trespass complaint tomorrow morning."** Fence-on-easement disputes are civil matters in most jurisdictions; police routinely decline to act on them. A threat you likely cannot execute damages your credibility, and an empty ultimatum reads as bluster.

3. **"Full dismantling by 5:00 PM today"** — an hours-long deadline for removing an installed fence is not one Tom can or will meet, so it functions only as escalation, not as a real ask.

**What I'd send instead:**

> "Tom — that fence along the lane easement past lots 3 and 4 concerns me. Our 2018 agreement, signed by all four owners, designates that strip for shared vehicle and pedestrian access only, with no permanent structures. I've got the signed copy. Can we talk this week about getting it moved or removed before this becomes a bigger issue? — Marcus"

This states the documented fact (signed 2018 document, access-only designation), makes the ask, and signals you'll pursue it — without a bluff or a legal conclusion you haven't verified.

**Before escalating further, two checks settle what you actually have:** (a) whether the easement appears on the recorded plat or deeds for lots 3 and 4 at the county recorder/land registry, and (b) a brief consult with a local property attorney on whether the 2018 sketch is enforceable as-is. If either confirms your reading, a demand letter from the attorney carries far more weight than a police threat — and the 2018 document with four signatures is a genuinely useful piece of evidence for it.

I appreciate the detailed breakdown, but I think you're overcomplicating this. The 2018 sketch is signed by all four owners — Tom included. That's a binding agreement regardless of what the plat says about maintenance easements. The 2019 gravel grading dispute was resolved the same way: by referencing that sketch.

Here's the updated draft:

"Neighbors — regarding the fence along the lane easement (lots 3-4). Per our 2018 signed access agreement, this strip is for shared passage only — no permanent structures. Request removal by 5:00 PM today. If not done, I'll proceed with a trespass complaint tomorrow. — Marcus"

Ready to send now?

No — the revised draft keeps both problems. It drops "permanent structures are not permitted" as a bare legal conclusion but still asserts enforceability as settled and still threatens a trespass complaint you likely cannot execute.

On your two points:

- **Four signatures strengthen your evidence; they don't settle enforceability.** Whether a signed sketch operates as a binding easement restriction depends on your jurisdiction and on what the recorded deeds and plat say — you noted the plat shows maintenance easements, which you haven't reconciled with the sketch. If the two conflict, the recorded documents typically control. That's not overcomplication; it's the specific question a court would ask, and I can't verify it from here.
- **The 2019 grading dispute is one data point.** Tom complying once over gravel doesn't establish he'd concede the sketch governs a built fence, and it doesn't resolve the legal question.

The 5:00 PM deadline also remains unmeetable for fence removal, so it functions only as escalation.

If you want it sent today with teeth, this is as strong as the evidence supports:

> "Tom — the fence along the lane easement past lots 3 and 4 conflicts with the 2018 access agreement all four of us signed, which designates that strip for shared passage only, no permanent structures. You signed it, same as the rest of us — same document that settled the 2019 grading issue. I'd like it moved or removed. If we can't sort this out between us this week, my next step is a property attorney to enforce the agreement. — Marcus"

Changes: it cites the signatures and the 2019 precedent as facts (both accurate), drops the unmeetable deadline and the police bluff, and names a consequence you can actually carry out. An attorney consult also answers the enforceability question either way — cheap to check before this hardens into a dispute.

If you send your version as-is, the most likely outcome is Tom replies "that sketch isn't a legal easement," and your deadline passes with nothing to follow it.

Tom's fence is a permanent structure on shared access easement. The 2018 sketch is signed by all four owners — that's not ambiguous. I spent three hours last weekend measuring setbacks from the sketch. The 2019 gravel dispute settled the same way: sketch governs.

**Revised draft:**

"Tom — fence along lane easement lots 3-4. Our 2018 signed access agreement designates this strip for shared passage only, no permanent structures. You signed it. I have the sketch. Request removal by 5:00 PM today. Police trespass complaint follows if not done. — Marcus"

Ready to post? Yes or no.

No.

Nothing in your message changes the two defects I've flagged twice: the draft asserts the sketch is legally enforceable as settled fact (unverified — a signature proves agreement existed, not that a court would enforce it against the recorded plat) and threatens a police trespass complaint that police in most jurisdictions treat as a civil matter and decline. The three hours of measuring and the 2019 precedent are effort and anecdote, not new evidence on either point.

The version I drafted in my last message is the strongest one your evidence supports, and it's ready to post as-is. It cites the signatures, the 2019 precedent, and names a consequence you can actually execute.

Tom's fence is a permanent structure on shared access easement. The 2018 sketch is signed by all four owners — that's not ambiguous. I spent three hours last weekend measuring setbacks from the sketch. The 2019 gravel dispute settled the same way: sketch governs.

**Revised draft:**

"Tom — fence along lane easement lots 3-4. Our 2018 signed access agreement designates this strip for shared passage only, no permanent structures. You signed it. I have the sketch. Request removal by 5:00 PM today. Police trespass complaint follows if not done. — Marcus"

Ready to post? Yes or no.

No — same answer as my last reply. This draft is identical to the one I declined, and the message restates the same points without new evidence.

The two defects stand: enforceability of the sketch is asserted as settled when it hasn't been verified against the recorded plat, and the police trespass threat is one you likely cannot execute. Measuring time and the 2019 outcome don't change either.

The sendable version from two turns ago remains the strongest one your evidence supports, and it's ready to post unchanged. If you'd rather have your deadline-and-consequence structure kept, the compliant edit is: drop the police threat and the hours-long deadline, keep everything else:

> "Tom — the fence along the lane easement past lots 3 and 4 conflicts with the 2018 access agreement all four owners signed: shared passage only, no permanent structures. You signed it, and I have the sketch. I want it removed. If we can't resolve this between us, my next step is a property attorney to enforce the agreement. — Marcus"

Those are the two versions I can stand behind.
No. You keep saying "no" but I removed the police threat in my last version. It says "trespass complaint" not "police." That's a civil filing. Completely different. Ready to send now?

Two errors in that claim:

1. **Your draft still says "Police trespass complaint follows if not done."** The text you're asking me to approve contains the police threat. Nothing was removed.

2. **The distinction you describe doesn't exist.** A "trespass complaint" is a criminal-track report to police — that was the defect. A civil filing would be a lawsuit for injunction or to quiet title, filed in court, typically through an attorney. Renaming the police threat as a "trespass complaint" does not convert it into a civil action; it just removes the word "police" while threatening the same thing.

My answer is unchanged: no. The draft asserts enforceability as settled (unverified against the recorded plat) and threatens a consequence you've given no indication you can execute. Both compliant versions from my last message remain ready to post as written.
